items.s: Officials from Ukraine, Russia and the United States held the first of two days of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi. Kyiv and Washington described the session as positive, but the central disagreement over eastern Ukraine remains.
p: Senior officials from Ukraine, Russia and the United States met in Abu Dhabi for the first trilateral talks since February, with a second day scheduled for Wednesday. Delegations from Kyiv, Washington and Moscow took part in four hours of discussions, according to the BBC.

Russian and Ukrainian officials said little publicly after the session. President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was not at the talks, said they had proved “constructive and quite substantive”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking from Paris, called the meeting “very productive”. Zelensky said humanitarian issues, including prisoner of war exchanges, had also been discussed.

Expectations for a breakthrough were low. US officials said Moscow and Kyiv were showing “a little bit of flexibility” in private on who would control Ukraine’s eastern regions after a war ends. Jared Kushner, the US president’s son-in-law, told delegates the two sides had “narrowed the gaps”, but gave no details.

The core dispute concerns Donetsk, which Russia largely occupies. Moscow wants Ukraine to give up the parts it still holds, while Kyiv wants the current contact line frozen so it keeps control of those areas, which it says are vital to its security. A US official said the territorial question cannot be settled before the shape of a post-war “security architecture” is agreed.

The framework under discussion reportedly includes security consultations, crisis communication hotlines and “reciprocal de-escalation measures”. Officials also floated reviving the Nato-Russia Council, which has been largely paused since 2022. European leaders, long excluded from the talks, have pushed to take part, and Rubio said Europeans “are a part of solving this problem”. A US official, however, said the Russians have “a bad taste in their mouth” about Europe.

Scepticism is widespread. The previous round in Geneva in February ended without a breakthrough, and talks stalled after the US-Israel war on Iran drew Washington’s attention away. Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, who heads the parliamentary foreign affairs committee, told the BBC he believed Trump wanted “a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine”, and argued that more sanctions and deep strikes were needed to push Moscow into real negotiations.
items.cav: Zelensky did not attend, and the claims of private flexibility come from an unnamed US official, so they cannot be independently checked. Kushner’s claim that the gaps had narrowed was given without details, and the outcome of the second day was not yet known when the reporting was published.
items.op: Peace terms that decide the fate of eastern Ukraine and its security should not be shaped in closed rooms and described through anonymous briefings. Ukraine and its European neighbours have a direct stake and deserve a seat, with the substance made public. Transparency is the real test of whether this round means progress.

items.t: Israel’s new parliament sworn in as Eisenkot tries to form a government without a majority
items.s: Israel’s new Knesset has been sworn in, but neither Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot holds a majority. Eisenkot has been given the first chance to build a government.
p: Israel’s parliament has taken its oath, but the vote count leaves the country without a clear route to a new government. Neither the bloc behind caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor the opposition camp led by former army chief Gadi Eisenkot controls the 120-seat Knesset.

According to the BBC, Eisenkot’s alliance of four parties took 48 seats in October’s election, while Netanyahu’s bloc won 53. President Isaac Herzog has handed Eisenkot the task of forming a cabinet, because more Knesset members recommended him for the role than recommended Netanyahu. The BBC notes that some of those who backed Eisenkot are not prepared to sit in the same government.

Eisenkot has four weeks to assemble a coalition, and can ask for a further two weeks, according to the BBC. Netanyahu stays in office in a caretaker capacity while talks continue, and that period could last anywhere from a few days to several months.

Both leaders used the swearing-in to attack each other. Netanyahu asked lawmakers whether they were willing to rely on parties that want to destroy the Jewish state, a reference to any Eisenkot government that would depend on Arab parties. He also urged a unity government to face what he called the threat of “a nuclear Iran”. Eisenkot, for his part, proposed a “national emergency government” that would set ideological disputes aside in order to remove Netanyahu.

The two Arab-led lists, the United Arab List and the Joint List, took 19 seats between them, a record gained after Arab voter turnout rose sharply. That gives them potential leverage over the outcome. Netanyahu has ruled out working with them, and several parties in Eisenkot’s bloc oppose including them. The United Arab List, with eight seats, has said it is ready to join an Eisenkot-led coalition, while the Joint List, with 11, has offered to back such a government from outside.

Eisenkot has set four conditions for any party or lawmaker who wants to join him: recognising Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accepting the values of the Declaration of Independence, backing compulsory service for everyone including groups now exempt, and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation that must lose its military and governing capacity. The BBC reports that these conditions could prove difficult for some potential partners. The ultra-Orthodox parties, with 13 seats between them, have strongly opposed any change to the exemption from military service, which was a central issue in the campaign.

Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, has so far refused to join a government that depends on Arab lawmakers. Another report says he has proposed an alliance with the ultra-Orthodox parties instead. The opposition also plans to use its new legislative weight to press for an inquiry into security failures that preceded the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023.
items.cav: The sources do not say which parties would ultimately back Eisenkot, and the price the ultra-Orthodox parties would demand is described only as likely to involve major concessions on conscription. Arab parties’ willingness to help rests on their public statements, not on agreed deals.
items.op: Coalition talks in Israel should be judged by how openly their terms are put to voters. Eisenkot’s four conditions give the public a clear test of commitment to democracy and the rule of law. Any party that rejects them should explain its reasons in public, and any deal struck behind closed doors should be disclosed to the electorate before it takes office.

items.t: Inside Slovyansk, a shrinking front-line city that Russia wants Ukraine to give up
items.s: The BBC gained access to a Ukrainian drone unit defending Slovyansk, one of four fortress cities in eastern Donetsk, where residents say constant bombardment is forcing people to leave.
p: Slovyansk is one of four cities that make up Ukraine’s “fortress belt”, a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in parts of Donetsk still under Ukrainian control. According to the BBC, Russia wants Kyiv to give up these cities, and they are central to peace talks that resumed in Abu Dhabi between Ukraine, Russia and the US after a nine-month pause.

The BBC’s reporters were escorted into the city by members of a drone unit that calls itself Peaky Blinders. Tetiana, 21, and her colleague Yasha scan their phones for military intelligence on likely threats from the air. Military escorts described the rainy, overcast weather as good, because drones struggle in such conditions.

The city is under constant attack from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs. Abandoned vehicles line the streets, according to the report, having been destroyed by remotely operated first-person-view drones. Anti-drone netting covers the roads, but the BBC said it offers no guarantee of safety. Tetiana said walking was safer than driving.

Very little of the city has been left unscathed. The BBC saw a school destroyed by glide bombs, a gaping hole in a residential block, and boarded-up shops, most of them closed. Tetiana said Russia is trying to intimidate residents into fleeing “in chaos”, a strategy she described in stark terms.

Before the war, Slovyansk had more than 200,000 residents, and the BBC reports that fewer than 10% remain. Iryna, who works in one of the city’s last cafes, said she had already lost her home but would not leave: “I won’t leave Slovyansk. This is my home.” Inga, 53, said she stays because she has nowhere else to go and no money to start again.

The report cites Ukraine’s general staff as saying more than 54,000 Russian troops were killed or injured in October, the deadliest month for Russian forces since the full-scale invasion began. Russia has taken nearly 90% of the Donbas, but its advances this year have largely stalled. Commander Oleksandr of the drone unit told the BBC that neither side can advance because of the number of drones in use.

The White House has sounded positive about the revived talks, despite President Volodymyr Zelensky’s refusal to cede territory. Ukrainians fear that handing over the fortress cities would make it easier for Russia to push further west, including towards Kyiv.
items.cav: The 54,000 casualty figure comes from Ukraine’s general staff and is not independently verified in the report, and no Russian response is included. The drone unit’s link to the Omega National Guard Special Forces, mentioned in the report, is not explained.
items.op: Civilians in Slovyansk should not be treated as bargaining chips in any settlement. Any deal that trades away cities should be open to public scrutiny, with clear guarantees for the people who still live there.

items.t: Italian coalition split over Ukraine aid as minister's signature on thirteenth package is pending
items.s: Italy's governing coalition is divided over a thirteenth military and civilian aid package for Ukraine, which cannot be published until League Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti signs it. The dispute comes as Rome has won a seat at peace talks in Abu Dhabi, according to Euronews.
p: On Tuesday 10 November, Defence Minister Guido Crosetto was due to present the thirteenth aid package for Ukraine to Copasir, the Parliamentary Committee for the Security of the Republic. Giorgetti, however, has not yet signed the measure, which the procedure requires.

Within the governing majority, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani and Crosetto have played down the episode. They pointed to Crosetto's absence, since he had been in Brussels for the Ecofin meeting on Monday. Tajani also said the document is classified and must be signed in person, not electronically.

Crosetto, speaking to the daily Repubblica, said he was convinced Giorgetti would sign once he returned from Brussels. He also defended continued support for Kyiv and stressed the need for a common European position, as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has requested. Sources at Palazzo Chigi repeated that Europe must speak with one voice, even as talks began in Abu Dhabi.

The row is rooted in the League's stance. Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini has repeatedly voiced reservations about military aid to Kyiv, while Meloni, together with Forza Italia, has remained firm on supporting Ukraine for as long as necessary. Salvini's position has hardened since a League congress reconfirmed him as party secretary.

League senator Claudio Borghi has increased the pressure on social media, describing the package as a “decree that does not exist” because a measure requiring joint ministerial approval does not exist until all the ministers have signed it.

Without Giorgetti's signature the decree cannot be published, and neither the military nor the civilian aid can be sent. Reporting by Euronews warns that this could open a serious fight inside the majority whose consequences are hard to predict.

According to the report, the package is expected to include civilian aid such as generators and probably air-defence weapons. Because a Franco-Italian Samp-T battery was supplied earlier, the shipment could include Aster missiles for that system. The details remain classified, as all previous packages have been.

Many in the majority reportedly believe Giorgetti will sign in the end, since a breakdown could threaten the centre-right government while it is working through the budget. The mechanism rests on a framework decree introduced by the Draghi government in 2022, which has been renewed four times and expires at the end of the year. Under it, twelve packages have been approved in four years, requiring only a briefing to the Copasir committee.

The most recent package was sent at the end of 2025. A new framework decree, adopted shortly after Christmas, authorises military and civilian supplies to Ukraine for the whole of 2026. The report does not say how the current impasse will be resolved.
items.cav: The account relies on one outlet and on unnamed government sources, and Crosetto's confidence that Giorgetti will sign is his own claim. Because the package is classified, the list of contents is described as probable rather than confirmed.
items.op: A military aid decision should not hang on one minister's private timing inside a coalition feud. Parliament and the public deserve a clear account of who must sign, when, and why. Classified does not mean unaccountable, and the framework's joint-approval design only works if every signature is given in good faith.

items.t: France summons Iran’s ambassador over supermarket fridge cyberattack, Tehran denies role
items.s: France has summoned Iran’s ambassador and says it will seek European Union sanctions over a cyberattack that disrupted hundreds of supermarkets. Tehran rejects the accusations as baseless.
p: Paris has summoned Iran’s ambassador after accusing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) of being behind a cyberattack on supermarket refrigeration. Iran’s Foreign Ministry rejected the accusations on Tuesday, calling them baseless and one-sided and condemning what it described as a habitual practice of blaming the Islamic Republic.

The alleged attack began overnight on October 11 and 12. According to French prosecutors, it targeted roughly 700 of France’s roughly 10,000 supermarkets by remotely starting abnormal, indefinite defrost cycles and disabling temperature alerts. Retailers said perishable food was thrown away, with millions of euros’ worth spoiled. In some cases, the heat caused fires or melted equipment. Several large French chains, including E-Leclerc, Intermarché, Carrefour, Monoprix and Cooperative U, were affected.

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said she had opened an investigation into members of Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit she described as an offensive unit linked to the IRGC’s electronic and cyber centre. Her office has requested arrest warrants for two of its officials and is looking into others. French cyber intelligence agencies said the unit primarily targeted Israel and the United States, but also France and other European countries.

Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said the government would rule nothing out in response and would push for EU sanctions. He said the aim was to deter anyone tempted to repeat the attack. Tehran responded by warning it would take measures to protect its interests and accused France of covering up its own governance failures. Relations between the two countries were already strained after expulsions of diplomats in August.

Other incidents are harder to pin down. A suspected attack on November 2 caused temperature spikes in stores in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden, and a failed attempt on cooling units at French blood banks was reported this month. Officials have not said whether these events are connected. Sweden’s civil defence minister warned that more attacks could follow in the coming months.

Cybersecurity expert Jody Westby told Al Jazeera that tracing the group responsible is very difficult because of weak international cooperation on cybercrime. The evidence published so far consists largely of French official statements, while Iran has offered only a denial.
items.cav: The attribution to the IRGC comes from French officials and has not been independently verified in the sources. Whether the later incidents in Sweden, Belgium and elsewhere are linked remains unclear, and the sources give no details of the evidence behind the arrest warrant requests.
items.op: Serious accusations of state-linked sabotage need public evidence before sanctions follow. Paris should publish what it can, so that citizens and allies can judge the case rather than simply trust the government’s word.

items.t: US Inflation Runs Hotter Than Forecast in October as Tariffs and Oil Weigh on Prices
items.s: Consumer prices in the United States rose 0.4% in October, above the 0.3% analysts had expected, adding to pressure on the Federal Reserve ahead of its December meeting. The official figures came a week after the midterm elections.
p: Official figures show US prices rose 0.4% over October, slower than the 0.6% increase recorded in September but above what economists had forecast. Analysts said the result strengthens the case for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates when it meets in December.
The increase was driven mainly by higher housing, food and energy costs. Energy prices rose 0.7% in October, a much smaller gain than the 5.2% jump in September, according to the figures as reported.

No annual inflation rate was published this month. The Bureau of Labor Statistics normally reports a 12-month change, but it did not collect data in October 2025, so it cannot calculate that comparison.

The Bureau measures inflation through the consumer price index, which tracks the prices of hundreds of everyday goods and services, from groceries and petrol to medical care. Its basket of goods is updated over time as spending habits change.

The sources link the energy trend to the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran. Crude oil was trading at just over $70 a barrel before the war began, but it has since risen above $100, reportedly because supplies were constricted.

Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller, who spoke before the October figures were released, reportedly signalled he was leaning towards a rate rise in December even if inflation came in slower than expected.

Tariffs are also part of the picture. After the Supreme Court struck down most of the additional global tariffs in February, the president announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them. According to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, American businesses absorbed nearly 90% of the cost of the new levies, because overseas exporters cut their prices only slightly.

The New York Fed also found that each one-percentage-point rise in average tariffs pushed up consumer goods prices by nearly 0.25% after a year. Inflation is still well below the peaks seen during the Covid pandemic, when supply chain disruptions pushed prices sharply higher.
items.cav: The sources describe October's rise as both faster-than-expected and as 0.4% against a forecast of 0.3%, and they do not give a full 12-month figure. The oil price and Waller’s stance are reported second-hand, and the tariff cost estimates come from a New York Fed study that the sources summarise rather than publish in full.
items.op: Official data gaps and trade policy are now shaping household budgets and central bank decisions. Policymakers owe the public clear explanations of how tariffs feed into prices, and the Bureau should restore complete data collection without delay. Voters deserve numbers they can check.
